ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - There was no celebration, but there was a revelation.
The Red Sox couldn't close the deal in securing a postseason berth, succumbing to a Rays 2-1 walk-off win at Tropicana Field on Saturday. But an interesting development emerged along the way. Brayan Bello is suddenly a potential huge part of the postseason solution.
The almost out-of-nowhere conversation about Bello's importance was given an enormous boost by one of the pitcher's best outings of his career. Not only did Bello hold the Rays to just one run over eight innings, but he also struck out 11 and walked no one.
Why was this even more impressive than simply the end-of-day box score? Because Bello managed all those punchouts, along with 17 whiffs, against a Rays team that has struck out fewer times than any club in baseball. No starting pitcher had managed double-digit strikeouts against Tampa Bay, with Toronto's Dylan Cease coming the closest with nine.
Bello matches his career high with 11 strikeouts! pic.twitter.com/NA2a2pDcAy
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 19, 2026
The dominance was just what the doctor ordered for Bello and the Red Sox, even if starting a postseason game isn't in the righty's immediate future.
While there has been no announcement, it appears the Red Sox are lining up their wild-card rotation with Payton Tolle to pitch Game 1 against the Yankees, followed by Sonny Gray and then Ranger Suarez if Game 3 is needed in the best-of-three series. But that doesn't mean Bello can't have an impact on outcomes from late September into October.
Bello's fastball routinely sat at 97 mph, almost two mph above his season-average velocity. It was a fastball that got nine whiffs, with the Rays coming away with just four hard-hit balls all day.
"That was exceptional," Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. "By far and away, his best outing of the year, as good as I've seen him, so, I don't know what else to say, he was awesome. Really awesome."
Bello's appearance allowed for thoughts on what might be in store for his effectiveness out of the bullpen in high-leverage situations come Sept. 29. It has been well-documented what he can do as a reliever, posting a 1.98 ERA in 15 games out of the bullpen this season. But now we're not just talking about bulk roles or giving the Red Sox some length.
This version of Bello can absolutely be a late-inning, high-leverage weapon.
For instance, while we aren't sure of Aaron Judge's health heading into the postseason, if the Yankees' slugger does play, this might not be a bad reminder to put in your statistical back pocket: Judge is just 2-for-21 with eight strikeouts against Bello.
While some naysayers might point to the less-than-inspiring appearances Bello has turned in at Yankee Stadium as of late, including maybe his worst relief outing of the season at the end of August when he allowed four runs over 4 1/3 innings, or the 2 1/3-inning start in Game 2 of last season's wild card round. But before those two, the pitcher had been absolutely nails in the Bronx, totaling a 1.44 ERA in five starts.
Assuming their health is OK, the Red Sox will have Aroldis Chapman and Garrett Whitlock at the ready to help close out games. But with a week to go in the regular season, there is some uncertainty regarding the late-inning options. Saturday, Bello sure seemed like he was ready to help with that.
“For me, it's just showing the team that I'm ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.”

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

Sep 20, 2026, 12:47 AM ET
WEEI's Rob Bradford reports that it is "sure looking like" Boston Red Sox left-hander Payton Tolle has a "good shot" at pitching Game 1 of a wild-card series to kick off the postseason with the way the Red Sox are lining things up. It means that the 23-year-old southpaw will not get a start this weekend against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays. The former second-rounder from TCU in 2024 has had a strong first full season in the big leagues with Boston in 2026, going 9-6 with a 3.02 ERA (3.04 FIP) and 1.07 WHIP with 166 strikeouts and 38 walks in 143 innings across his 25 starts. Another lefty, Patrick Sandoval, is now scheduled to make the start for the BoSox in the series finale in Tampa. Tolle allowed four earned runs in 5 2/3 innings against the Seattle Mariners on Aug. 31, but he has only given up one earned run with one walk and 19 punchouts in 12 innings across his last two starts against the Baltimore Orioles and Kansas City Royals in September.--Keith Hernandez
Source: WEEI - Rob Bradford
More Recent News
Xavier Edwards Leaves Early on Saturday With Thumb Discomfort


Keith Hernandez




Sep 20, 2026, 12:31 AM ET
Miami Marlins infielder Xavier Edwards (thumb) left Saturday night's game at Petco Park against the San Diego Padres early with discomfort in his left thumb, according to Christina De Nicola. The Marlins' training staff was checking Edwards' left hand out when he fouled a ball off in the seventh frame. It is worth noting that Edwards previously missed time this season with a sprained left thumb, which he might have aggravated on Saturday night. Before leaving the ballgame, Edwards went 0-for-3 with a walk and two strikeouts. He was replaced at the keystone in San Diego by Jared Serna. If the 27-year-old switch-hitting middle infielder did aggravate his left-thumb sprain, there is a good chance that he will not play again for the Marlins in the final week of the 2026 season. Edwards came into Wednesday's contest with a nice .282/.361/.373 slash line with a .733 OPS, a career-high six home runs, a career-high 52 RBI, 61 runs scored, and 21 stolen bases in 141 games played. He has stolen 20-plus bases in each of the last three seasons, including a career-high 31 back in 2024.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Christina De Nicola
Aaron Judge Hopes to be Back for Postseason, No Timetable Given


Keith Hernandez




Sep 20, 2026, 12:23 AM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge (calf) said on Saturday that his right-calf strain is in the soleus muscle, according to Bryan Hoch of MLB.com. However, Judge would not say what grade of strain his MRI exam revealed. "I'd like to be back by the postseason. That's definitely the plan. I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that," Judge said. The New York Daily News' Gary Phillips reports that neither Judge nor manager Aaron Boone has shared much information on his injury, with the Yankees treating his calf strain like "classified CIA intel." "It doesn't matter what grade it is," Boone said. "We're at nine games left [in the season]." Because we have no idea of the exact severity of his calf injury, it is entirely plausible that Judge could miss most, or all, of any potential Yankees playoff run in October. Judge has been throwing, working out, and getting treatment, and he said he is "gonna do everything we can do to get back as soon as we can." Boone, though, merely said he is "hoping for the best." It will be difficult for the Yankees to go all the way if they do not get Judge back for the playoffs. It has been a frustrating year for the three-time MVP and all of his fantasy managers, as he has only played in 66 games due to a stress fracture in his rib, slashing .241/.360/.511 with 18 home runs, 41 RBI, 45 runs, and five steals.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Bryan Hoch
Roki Sasaki to Return Next Week


Andy Webb




Sep 19, 2026, 10:37 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Roki Sasaki (finger) will make his return to the mound next week during the series against the San Diego Padres, David Vassegh reports. Sasaki looked good during his side session on Wednesday, so the Dodgers have cleared him to get back on the mound. It doesn't sound like the Dodgers have decided whether Sasaki will start or come out of the bullpen during his outing against the Padres. The right-hander has been out since late August due to a finger blister. The expectation is that Sasaki will likely pitch in a bullpen role for the team during the postseason.--Andy Webb
Source: David Vassegh
Trey Yesavage to Start on Monday


Andy Webb




Sep 19, 2026, 10:31 PM ET
Toronto Blue Jays starting pitcher Trey Yesavage (knee) is scheduled to start against the Baltimore Orioles on Monday, Arden Zwelling of Sportsnet.ca reports. Yesavage has been out since August after having surgery to repair a torn meniscus in his right knee. He only made one rehab appearance at Triple-A Buffalo before getting cleared to pitch for the big league club. The Jays plan to have Yesavage pitch roughly three innings or around 45 to 50 pitches. Spencer Miles is expected to take over for the bulk of the innings after Yesavage is done. It'll be interesting to see if the Jays decide to shut down Yesavage if they do get eliminated from playoff contention. Until then, it sounds like the right-hander is going to contribute here soon.--Andy Webb
Source: Arden Zwelling
Cal Quantrill Removed with Lat Tightness


Andy Webb




Sep 19, 2026, 10:22 PM ET
Texas Rangers starting pitcher Cal Quantrill (lat) exited early during Saturday's outing against the Toronto Blue Jays. Quantrill was pulled out in the second inning due to right lat tightness, Kennedi Landry of MLB.com reports. He was able to record four outs before exiting this contest. Jordan Montgomery took over on the mound and threw 3.2 scoreless innings. Quantrill figures to undergo an MRI, so fantasy managers will likely have to wait for the results on that. Nathan Eovaldi could be asked to move back into the starting rotation if Quantrill is forced to miss time. UPDATE: The Dallas Morning News' Shawn McFarland reports that Quantrill will undergo an MRI exam on Sunday morning, per manager Skip Schumaker.--Andy Webb
Source: Kennedi Landry
Sep 19, 2026, 10:15 PM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Spencer Jones (foot) was not in the starting lineup ahead of Saturday's game against the Arizona Diamondbacks. The Yankees decided to rest Jones on Saturday due to left foot/heel soreness, according to Brendan Kuty of The Athletic. It sounds like a day-to-day issue, so the Yankees are just going to play it safe. Jones is 1-for-19 with nine strikeouts over his last four games, so he could probably use a day off to rest and reset. Jose Caballero takes over in center field for Saturday's game. Fantasy managers should check back ahead of Sunday's game for another update on Jones.--Andy Webb
Source: Brendan Kuty
Shohei Ohtani Takes Simulated At-Bats


Andy Webb




Sep 19, 2026, 10:05 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani (knee, biceps) has progressed to taking simulated at-bats off the team's pitching machine on Saturday, Jack Harris of the California Post reports. Ohtani was also able to run the bases as he works his way back from a biceps and knee issue. It's unclear if Ohtani will return when he's first eligible on Wednesday. The Dodgers have already clinched the postseason, so they don't exactly need to rush him back into the lineup. However, the Dodgers would probably like for Ohtani to play in a few regular-season games before the playoffs begin. Fantasy managers should check back for another update in a few days.--Andy Webb
Source: Jack Harris
Jac Caglianone Returning to Saturday's Lineup


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 5:54 PM ET
Kansas City Royals first baseman/outfielder Jac Caglianone (hand) is serving as the designated hitter and is batting third in Saturday's contest on the road against the Pittsburgh Pirates and right-hander Bubba Chandler, per MLB.com. Caglianone suffered a minor hand injury before Friday's series opener at PNC Park, but he is back in action on Saturday and should be returned to fantasy lineups against a right-hander, despite his cold streak of late. The 23-year-old former first-rounder has produced a .277/.328/.483 slash line with an .811 OPS, 23 home runs, 70 RBI, 66 runs scored, and six stolen bases in 484 at-bats in 2026 in his first full big-league season with the Royals. Cags was red-hot in August, slashing .411/.429/.684 with a 1.113 OPS, six home runs, eight doubles, 26 RBI, 17 runs scored, and three stolen bases in 24 games, but he has been banged up in September and has gone just 4-for-27 (.148) with zero homers, four RBI, one walk, and 11 strikeouts. He has never faced Chandler in the majors.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sebastian Walcott to be Promoted to Triple-A


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 3:01 PM ET
Texas Rangers top infield prospect Sebastian Walcott is expected to be promoted to Triple-A Round Rock on Saturday, according to Kennedi Landry of MLB.com. Walcott will make his debut as the designated hitter on Saturday night. The No. 9 overall prospect in all of baseball, per MLB Pipeline, has only played in 39 games in the minors this year after having surgery on his UCL, but since returning, he has slashed .322/.398/.586 with nine home runs and 11 stolen bases in 37 games for Double-A Frisco. In a playoff series with the Rough Riders, Walcott went 4-for-11 with a homer and four stolen bases. Walcott is only 20 years old, but if he continues to ascend and looks good in spring training next year, he could push for an early-season MLB promotion for the Rangers. It is impossible to ignore his 40-homer upside at the shortstop position in fantasy baseball, which makes him a must-stash already in dynasty/keeper leagues.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Kennedi Landry
Orioles Shutting Ryan Helsley Down


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 1:40 PM ET
The Baltimore Orioles are shutting down right-handed reliever Ryan Helsley (elbow) for the rest of the season, general manager Mike Elias told Andy Kostka of The Baltimore Banner. The focus is on Helsley getting ready for next season. Elias said that Helsley is not dealing with a new injury, but the debate was over contracting his buildup timeline, and the O's opted against that. In related news, the Orioles reinstated right-handed reliever Felix Bautista (shoulder) from the 60-day injured list, and he will join the team's active roster for the first time since July of last year after he had surgery to fix a torn labrum and rotator cuff in his shoulder. Helsley's first year in Baltimore was a lost cause due to his elbow issues, as he was able to throw only 15 1/3 innings, going 0-4 with a 4.11 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 21 strikeouts, and eight saves in 17 appearances. He will not be a lock to open the 2027 campaign as Baltimore's primary closer, especially with Bautista now back and healthy.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Baltimore Banner - Andy Kostka
Willson Contreras Still Out on Saturday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 1:04 PM ET
Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras (hand) remains out of the team's starting lineup for Saturday's contest against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays for the second straight day, per MLB.com. Nick Sogard will make another start at first base and will bat fifth against Rays right-hander Freddy Peralta. Contreras was diagnosed with a bruised right hand after leaving Thursday's game against the Texas Rangers after he was hit by a pitch. X-rays came back negative, though, so he is considered day-to-day and could make his return in Sunday's series finale in Tampa. Fantasy managers are hoping to get the 34-year-old Venezuelan back in their starting lineups as soon as possible, as the four-time All-Star has hit a career-high 27 home runs while driving in 81 runs in 129 games and 533 plate appearances in his first year with the club. Various injuries have limited Contreras to only four games so far in September, though, and he has gone 4-for-12 with a homer and two RBI.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Aroldis Chapman Won't Pitch This Weekend


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 11:07 AM ET
Boston Red Sox left-handed closer Aroldis Chapman (lat) felt some tightness in his lat while working out before Tuesday's game against the Texas Rangers and has not pitched since. Chapman said that he will not pitch this weekend against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays, but he expects to return during the final homestand of the regular season, which starts on Tuesday, according to Ian Browne of MLB.com. The veteran southpaw downplayed the injury on Friday, saying that the Red Sox are being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the series opener against the Rays, but the team told him not to. "I'm not worried at all," Chapman said. "From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time." Fantasy managers will be without Chapman this weekend, but for championship matchups next week, he will hopefully be ready to return to ninth-inning duties. The 38-year-old has been excellent in 2026 in his second year in Boston, posting a 1.95 ERA with a 1.14 WHIP, 34 saves, and 68 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings pitched. Right-hander Garrett Whitlock should handle a save situation this weekend if it arises in Tampa.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Ian Browne
Justin Verlander Throws Live Batting Practice


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 10:03 AM ET
Detroit Tigers starting pitcher Justin Verlander (hamstring/hip) threw a one-inning, 20-pitch live batting practice session on Friday. The 43-year-old said that he felt great after this successful outing. This was yet another step in the right direction, as it was his first time throwing against live batters. What lies ahead in his progress remains to be seen, as the plan is for him to pitch one final time in his illustrious career on Saturday, September 26, against the Pittsburgh Pirates. Whether or not he is able to throw one inning or more remains questionable, but with him retiring after this season, chances are he will be healthy enough to make that appearance and cap off one of baseball's greatest careers. With 266 wins and 3,554 strikeouts over 21 seasons, the surefire Hall of Famer will be looking to finish his career where it started: in Detroit.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Chris McCosky
Trent Grisham Could Return This Season


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 9:56 AM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Trent Grisham (hamstring) is pretty far into his recovery, two weeks after being placed on the 10-Day Injured List with a Grade 2 hamstring strain. Manager Aaron Boone reiterated that a return for him "could be in play" for the latter part of the season. It was also mentioned that when he does return, the Yankees would need to decide between him and Spencer Jones to play center field. This could complicate things for both players, as there could be some sort of platoon involving the two, diminishing their fantasy value down the stretch. Either way, the Yankees will be looking to solidify their lineup for the playoffs, and Grisham's fantasy value is very limited down the stretch, with or without a return before the playoffs.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Brendan Kuty - The Athletic
Tristan Peters Dealing With Multiple Injuries


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 9:39 AM ET
Chicago White Sox outfielder Tristan Peters (rib/shoulder) crashed into the wall during Friday's game while trying to catch a fly ball in the outfield. He exited the game with contusions to both his ribs and shoulders, and Braden Montgomery took his place in the outfield. The good news is that he is listed as day-to-day and has no head injury, which was the initial concern at the time of impact. It's unclear if he will miss any time before returning, but with the White Sox in the middle of a divisional race, they may need his help sooner rather than later. The 26-year-old is hitting .272 on the season with 12 home runs and eight stolen bases, and is worth rostering in deep leagues.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Chicago White Sox
Justin Steele Completes Two-Inning Rehab Outing


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 9:30 AM ET
Chicago Cubs pitcher Justin Steele (elbow) threw a 33-pitch, two-inning rehab outing on Friday for the Triple-A Iowa Cubs. This was his fifth appearance since beginning his rehab assignment and the fourth that has been two innings in length. Arguably his most impressive outing yet, Steele walked the first batter of the game before striking out the side. He would finish with five strikeouts in total while not allowing a hit. While the velocity on his fastball sat at 90.2 miles per hour, it was his slider that impressed the most, generating four whiffs. It's unclear what lies ahead for him, as the Cubs are in the middle of a race for the Wild Card. While they have a comfortable lead on the teams chasing them, they do need to prepare for the postseason, and Steele returning to the Cubs may not be in the cards. What's clear is that he is feeling much better than he has in quite some time, and any return to the Cubs would likely be for a peace-of-mind appearance to allow him to enter the postseason on a healthy note, giving him the opportunity to work on coming back even stronger next spring. Fantasy managers should not expect much from him down the stretch, but those in dynasty leagues should take note and add him while they can.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Jason Kempf
Bryce Eldridge Expected to Play on Saturday

item.content:encoded:
There were many questions the New York Yankees needed Spencer Jones to answer this season. Now, we've seen enough of him, even if it's been in a couple of disjointed stints, to get a good idea of who he is at the major league level.
The answer: pretty damn good. After struggling early, Jones has found his footing. A big reason for his ascendancy has been surprising. The Vanderbilt product has mashed left-handed pitching.
He's now logged 51 plate appearances against lefties and has slashed an eye-watering .435/.490/.761 following his homer off Minnesota Twins lefty specialist Taylor Rodgers on Sept. 15. It was the first dinger Rodgers gave up to a left-handed hitter over 133 plate appearances this season.
The sample size isn't huge, but it's relatively significant. For example, Ben Rice has 209 plate appearances against lefties out of his 622 plate appearances. For Jones, the 51 matchups against southpaws are a decent portion of his 255 total plate appearances.
One of the most impressive things about how he's performed against same-handed pitching is the amount of power he's demonstrated. Obviously, the six-foot-seven outfielder is a behemoth, but most lefties, even those who perform well against southpaws, see a drop in power in those situations. Take Rice, for instance; his slugging percentage drops from .561 against righties to .457 against left-handers. That hasn't been the case for Jones.
This has just been one part of Jones' maturation process that should have every fan feeling confident about not only his future, but his ability to contribute now.
Spencer Jones' performance against lefties has Yankees well-positioned for playoffs vs. Red Sox
Overall, Jones is hitting .259/.331/.452 with 10 homers on the season. He's been even better since being recalled on July 22, posting a .271/.337/.490 line with eight of his 10 homers coming during this most recent span.
There should be no more doubt that he should start over Trent Grisham, assuming Grisham is healthy, once the playoffs roll around. A significant part of that reasoning has to do with his performance against southpaws.
Jones has learned a lot from Cody Bellinger on how to handle those tough at-bats since he's been up in the bigs and the star left fielder has been healthy.
“When we are in the dugout, he’s one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, ‘Yo, what did you see?’ He’ll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he’s going to do next time. It’s like, all right, good to know before I go even into my first (at-bat) what this MVP is going to do for his first at-bat. It’s pretty sweet knowing that I’ve got these guys to help me out,” Jones said to The Athletic this week.
He couldn't have a better mentor. Bellinger isn't hitting lefties as much as he did last year, when he put up an insane .353/.415/.601 line, but his .287/.346/.449 performance in 2026 is plenty good, and better than what he's done against righties. In fact, Bellinger is about as balanced as they come with an .804 career OPS against left-handers and an .819 mark against righties.
We spoke about Rice earlier, but the early-season drama about his usage against lefties is a thing of the past. While he has more pop against righties, Rice's .255/.330/.457 line against southpaws is more than serviceable.
Despite having so many lefties in the lineup on a daily basis, the Yankees as a whole don't suffer much from it. The club is hitting a collective .247/.318/.422 against left-handed pitching this season, with a .740 OPS that ranks ninth. Remember, for most of that time, Aaron Judge hasn't been a factor, either.
Looking ahead, the Yankees' most likely opponent in the Wild Card series is the Red Sox, who are loaded with left-handers. In the rotation, they boast southpaws Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez, with their being a possibility that Jake Bennett makes the cut, too. In the bullpen, they'll hope to unleash Garrett Crochet, Erik Miller and old friend Aroldis Chapman.
However, rather than being overmatched, we might say that this plays into the Yankees' hands. New York can handle left-handed pitching, and those lefty bats can tee off against righties. Jones emerging as a threat against southpaws only solidifies the strength and gives the Yankees another regular who doesn't need a platoon partner, allowing them to match up only where they're vulnerable.

There's a version of this continuous Boston Red Sox news saga that could have sent fans into a real panic, and I get why. Justin Slaten had quietly turned into one of the more trustworthy arms in this bullpen, working to a 2.84 ERA over his final two months of availability before elbow trouble sidelined him in August.
Now we know the full picture: an evaluation revealed degenerative changes in the flexor mass of his right elbow, and rather than push for a return with the postseason approaching, the Red Sox are having him get a PRP injection and start planning for 2027 instead.
On the year, he had thirty-six appearances, a 4.60 ERA overall, but provided a real chunk of high-leverage relief work, which is now gone for the stretch run. That's a real hole, absolutely. It's also not the whole story right now, and it's worth taking a breath before assuming the bullpen just got worse.
Garrett Crochet was the AL Cy Young runner-up last season, an 18-5, 2.59 ERA workhorse who threw 205.1 innings and struck out 255 batters. What a lot of people forget is that before all of that, Crochet broke into pro ball as a reliever with the Chicago White Sox, sitting comfortably in the upper 90s and regularly touching triple digits in short bursts. That's exactly the version the Red Sox may get back down the stretch.
He hasn't pitched in a game since throwing six scoreless innings on April 25, and after months sidelined with a shoulder issue that turned into more of a lingering problem, he just threw his first bullpen sessions in nearly three months. There isn't time left to stretch him back out as a starter, but a Crochet who can air it out for one to three innings at a time is exactly the profile that's thrived in October before.
Pair that with a Payton Tolle start going five or six innings, Crochet bridging the seventh and eighth, and Aroldis Chapman closing it out, and that's a real, dangerous alignment behind Sonny Gray in a Game 1.
Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo are trending toward returns to Red Sox bullpen alongside Garrett Crochet
Crochet isn't walking through that door alone, either. Tanner Houck is further along than anyone, working back from UCL surgery and already up to three innings and 48 pitches in a rehab outing for Double-A Portland, allowing just one run with four strikeouts, before moving on to Triple-A Worcester to keep building and facing some better competition.
Johan Oviedo, who Boston acquired from the Pittsburgh Pirates over the winter, finally made his own rehab appearance with Worcester this week after missing more than five months with a flexor strain, which is a sign he could factor into the bullpen picture before the year is out. Kutter Crawford is the longer shot of the group, hasn't pitched for the big club since 2024, and there are only unconfirmed "rumblings" he could get a look at Worcester this week. Even if that goes nowhere in 2026, he's still under team control for two more seasons.
Losing Slaten hurts, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But between Crochet, Houck, and Oviedo all trending in the right direction at the same time, Boston may be walking into the stretch run with more usable, high-upside arms than it's had healthy at any single point all season.

We're just over one week away from the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season coming to a close. Then, the entire focus around the league will turn to the playoffs. When it comes to the Boston Red Sox, they will be in the mix.
The Red Sox haven't officially clinched yet, although that could happen as soon as Saturday. As the playoffs have inched closer and closer, one topic that has lingered around Boston is the starting rotation. The rotation is loaded and it's a real question of how the club will sort it out ahead of a Wild Card round series, very likely against the New York Yankees. Sonny Gray has seemed like the likely choice, but that may not be the case.
Could Boston Turn To The Rookie?
Do you roll with the veteran in Game 1? He has been among the best pitchers in the league in general all season to this point. Ranger Suárez has been red-hot recently and was brought to town because of the fact that he has been electric in the playoffs throughout his career to this point. Also, of course, there's Payton Tolle, who is also red-hot right now. On Saturday, Rob Bradford of WEEI shared on X that Tolle actually has a "good shot" at nabbing the Game 1 spot.
"It sure looking like Tolle has a good shot at pitching Game 1 the way they are lining things up," Bradford wrote on X.
Gray has been among the best pitchers in baseball this season. He has a 2.82 ERA and a 146-to-45 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 163 innings pitched this season. Gray also is leading the league with 17 wins. He has been Boston's ace all season. Since Aug. 15, Gray has a 2.89 ERA and a 3-2 record. Since Sep. 4, Suárez has a 0.92 ERA and a 3-0 record. Since Aug. 13, Tolle has a 2.50 ERA and a 42-to-9 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 36 innings pitched across six starts.
Frankly, Boston would be in a good position with any of these three starting Game 1. But in a three-game series, there are even more reasons to get the decision right.
Tolle has made two starts against New York this season and has allowed one run in 13 innings pitched (0.69 ERA) with 18 strikeouts. Gray has made two starts against New York and has allowed three runs in 13 2/3 innings pitched (1.98 ERA) with 12 strikeouts.
Suárez has made three starts against New York and has allowed 11 runs in 16 1/3 innings pitched (5.94 ERA. Of the three, Tolle has fared the best against New York, so the fact that he has a "good shot" at starting Game 1 actually makes a lot of sense.
All three of these guys are red-hot at the moment. Slotting in Tolle for a Game 1, the righty Gray for a Game 2 and then back to a lefty in Suárez for Game 3 — if necessary — arguably is the best bet for a New York series.

item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray? Ranger Suarez? Payton Tolle? Who should get the ball in game one in the Bronx for the Red Sox?
To manage the starting rotation workload and line up the rotation for the playoffs, the Boston Red Sox are turning to Brayan Bello to start Saturday's game against the Tampa Bay Rays. Whether the Red Sox go with Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, or Payton Tolle, the team will feel very good about its chances of winning. However, if the team gets swept, it risks leaving an incredible arm on the bench.
Let's take a look at the argument for each of the trio to get the ball in game one:
Gray
The 36-year-old veteran has inarguably been the Red Sox' best starter in 2026. After entering the season with questions about how effective he could be late in his career, Gray has passed every test with flying colors. In 28 starts, Gray has posted a 2.82 ERA, the eighth-lowest mark in the league, while the Red Sox have gone 20-8 on his start days.
Most importantly, even when he doesn't have his best stuff, he has done well to limit damage; of his 28 starts, he has allowed more than three runs on four occasions. In two starts against the New York Yankees in 2026, Gray has allowed only three earned runs on nine hits, while striking out 12 and walking only four. In his career, Gray has a solid record of playoff success, posting a 3.26 ERA in 30.1 innings.
However, when it comes to elite strikeout stuff that can completely shut down a lineup, Gray lacks that, posting a rather pedestrian strikeouts per nine innings of 8.06, which ranks 30th out of 48 qualified starters.
Still though, Gray appears to be the most obvious choice to get the start in game one.
Suarez
The Red Sox' most difficult decision with their postseason rotation may be the one they have to make with Suarez. The 30-year-old All-Star signed a five-year, $130-million deal with the Red Sox in the offseason, in part because he posted an impressive 1.48 ERA over 42.2 innings with the Philadelphia Phillies.
However, of the trio in consideration, Suarez has been the shakiest since the All-Star break, posting a 3.46 ERA in his last 10 starts. However, the three-time All-Star has been better lately, allowing only two earned runs in 19.2 innings across three starts. Suarez has struggled against the Yankees in three starts in 2026, allowing 11 runs on 20 hits for a 6.06 ERA.
Still, it seems unlikely the team would risk leaving its $130 million investment on the sidelines for a playoff series.
Tolle
The 23-year-old rookie has been Boston's best starter since the All-Star break. In his last 10 starts, Tolle has posted a 2.90 ERA while striking out 12.05 batters per nine innings, the fifth-highest mark among 93 pitchers with at least 50 innings pitched.
Tolle has also performed incredibly well against the Yankees, allowing only one earned run on four hits while striking out 18 and walking only four. Tolle is also the only pitcher on the Boston staff with the electric stuff that could match New York ace Cam Schlittler in shutting down the lineup.
While it certainly may seem risky to some to give a 23-year-old rookie the ball in game one in Yankee Stadium, how can you risk not throwing him at all?
Up next for the Sox
With their magic number down to two, the Red Sox will look to win a series against the likely American League East champion Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday afternoon. Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.74 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) will start for Tampa. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 4:10 p.m. ET.

With the New York Yankees likely to face off against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, they will look to find any advantage they can to come out on top. That includes trying to gameplan against pitcher Payton Tolle, who will most likely be one of the Red Sox starters in the three-game set.
There's no question that Tolle is one the league's best and brightest young pitchers. Not only can he dominate a game, but he's so dang likeable that it's almost impossible to hate him. But that doesn't mean he's perfect.
Okay, he can be close to perfect sometimes, though. That's part of the problem. The Red Sox pitcher dazzled in the first inning in his Sept. 13 start against the Kansas City Royals. He threw the most smile-filled immaculate inning you’ll probably ever see, mainly utilizing his elite four-seam fastball. As his strongest pitch, he is using the four-seamer 45% of the time throughout his starts in 2026. And batters are hitting just .190 off of his heater on the season.
However, as the game against the Royals wore on, so did Tolle. His fastball velocity showed signs of dropping later in his start. While that's not too surprising for a starting pitcher, it could also be something for the Yankees to monitor. If they can work counts and force Tolle to throw a lot of pitches as he approaches a new and uncertain innings threshold, they may be able to sap his effectiveness early. The Royals start, as brilliant as it began, actually provided the Yankees with a blueprint.
The Yankees did not have luck against Tolle earlier this season
The Yankees are 1-1 against the Red Sox in games started by Tolle this season. However, he faced little resistance against the lineup in his two starts. On April 23, Tolle allowed just one run on three hits in six innings while striking out 11 batters. The Yankees scored three runs once Tolle left the game and picked up the win in Boston.
Two months later, Tolle pitched a seven-inning gem on June 26, once again at Fenway Park. He surrendered just one hit and two walks, striking out seven en route to a 6-1 Red Sox win. Nearly three months later, the Yankees will look to reverse their fortunes against the lefty. After a long season, the result could look a little differently for Tolle.
The 23-year-old has never thrown as many innings in a collegiate or professional season as he has in 2026. In fact, at 143 innings this season, he has pitched more than 50 innings over his previous career high. Now, you could look over at Cam Schlittler and say the thing, and you'd be correct. However, Schlittler’s velo hasn't trended downwards in a game as much as Tolle’s did on September 13.
To start the game, Tolle was consistently hitting 97 MPH with his four-seamer, a modest increase from his season average of 96.1 MPH. But by the sixth inning, his four-seam fastball was clocked as low as 92.7 MPH. Tolle still remained very effective, getting through the game without allowing a run and striking out seven. It's hard to say for certain if the wear and tear of a long MLB season is taking its toll on Tolle, but it could benefit a Yankees' lineup that has had mixed results against the fastball all season.
With an .845 slugging percentage against the heater, Ben Rice is by far the team's best batter when facing the cheese. He will look to set the tone early and jump on Tolle’s four-seamer. Luis García Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt have also raked against the fastball all season, though García Jr. has not hit as well against lefties. With Aaron Judge returning from injury and slowly returning to form, the team will have a decent advantage against any and all Red Sox fastballs, even Tolle's.
However, hitters like Cody Bellinger and Austin Wells will remain massive wild cards for the Yankees in the postseason. Each player has struggled to find success against the fastball in 2026. And if Jazz Chisholm Jr. is healthy enough to return to the lineup, his .338 slugging percentage will be the lowest of any starting position player. It'll be interesting to see which of these trends continues against Tolle’s fastball.
To add a hint of intrigue to the series, New York could also be facing off against another one of Boston's strong LHP. The Red Sox will gingerly work Garrett Crochet back into the mix, though he will also likely be on a pitch limit. It's not certain how the team will utilize Crochet, but he could certainly be a dangerous weapon for them, especially if paired with Tolle.
With Tolle already off to a great start in his career against the Yankees, he could continue his success this postseason. But with arm fatigue as a potential issue moving forward, his elite four-seam fastball may become just a little less overpowering. That's something that the Yankees could jump on.

Boston Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy knows his team has figured out the Tampa Bay Rays pretty well this season.
That said, the Red Sox (84-70) still can learn more about the Rays (93-60) when the teams meet Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
"At this point with (the Rays), we've played them enough already," Tracy said. "We have a pretty good understanding of them, (and) they have a pretty good understanding of us. But you could always pick up more stuff."
In Friday's series opener, the Red Sox scored four runs over the first three innings and won 4-2 to snap Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak and improve to 6-5 this season vs. the Rays.
Boston currently holds the second wild-card position in the American League but is dealing with several injuries.
"We have guys beat up that aren't here, and the hope is we get people healthy, and the roster could look even different a week from now than it does right now," Tracy said.
Boston's Willson Contreras is day-to-day after getting hit on the hand, while closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) has been unavailable the past two contests.
Right-hander Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery in 2025) and lefty Garrett Crochet (left shoulder inflammation) have advanced in their rehab assignments.
Boston left-hander Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02 ERA) is expected to make his 26th start on Saturday and will try to record his sixth consecutive win.
Tolle is 1-0 with an 0.75 ERA over 12 innings in his last two starts, allowing one run on eight hits while striking out 19 with a walk. He is 0-2 with a 4.50 ERA in two starts and one relief outing against Tampa Bay, which already has clinched a playoff berth.
Whatever Rays pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the rest of the staff have done with trade-deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta certainly has been a success.
Acquired by the club from the New York Mets for three prospects on Aug. 2, Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) -- a right-hander who will start for the Rays on Saturday -- arrived from the Big Apple as a lesser version of what he was during his two All-Star seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers.
He was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA with the Mets, but the work was immediately put in by the Rays to adjust Peralta to where he was when he was a 17-game winner with a sub-3.00 ERA last season.
"For some reason, when I got here, when I sat here with Kyle and (bullpen coach Jorge Moncada) and (manager Kevin Cash), they told me, like, 'You're gonna do what you want to do here, and we are going to help you to do it,'" Peralta said.
"And we know what you need to do to make those adjustments. We just put everything on the table. I just followed all the instructions, and it's what I am right now."

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter.
This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week from Tuesday and once again in the Bronx, the pitching plans look nothing like they did back then.
Which is good news for the Red Sox.
Even with Crochet sidelined all season by injury, the pitching rotation has been, in the words of interim manager Chad Tracy, “pivotal” to the drastic midseason turnaround that lifted this team from the depths of the American League standings and into the playoff race.
A trade for Sonny Gray. The continued development of Payton Tolle. And the free agent signing of Ranger Suarez. Three big moves, three likely starters for one more entry in the ongoing Boston/New York postseason clash of baseball titans.
Friday night in Florida, it was Suarez’s turn to prove his readiness. Facing the first-place Rays presented an obvious test, but for Suarez, it also was a chance to build on his two previous starts, in which he allowed only one run in 14 innings. As Tracy pointed out before the game, there is no mystery into what makes a good Suarez outing. Control the tempo, get ahead in the count, and locate pitches. When the lefthander does those three things, he can be pretty hard to beat.
But, as the Rays learned Friday, even if he doesn’t quite do those three things as well as he wants to, he can still find a way to battle through.
So there he was at the end of a decidedly mixed bag of a night, leading the Sox to a 4-2 win, improving his record to 8-4 after giving up just one run in 5⅔ innings. On the upside, he struck out five and consistently got key outs in key moments.
On the downside, he had to labor mightily to get there, walking a career-high five batters, throwing just 56 of his 98 pitches for strikes. He got away with it this time, but come the playoffs, that’s playing with fire, whether against the Yankees or perhaps the Rays again, with Tampa Bay in line to host the wild-card winners.
The Sox chose to take the positive out of the night.
“When I issued those walks, I think that the game was taking me to a place that wasn’t the right one. So I just tried to take a deep breath and slow it down, and I was able to then take it from there,” Suarez said.
He struck out Yandy Díaz to end the second inning, stranding two runners on base. He got out of another jam in the third, a Chandler Simpson hard-hit line out to right and a strikeout of Jonny DeLuca to strand two more runners.
Suarez did it again in the fourth, helping his own cause by starting a nifty inning-ending double play, snaring Taylor Walls’s line drive to the mound and then throwing to first to double off Nick Fortes.
A clean fifth ended on a called third strike to Junior Caminero, but gave way to a messier sixth, with a leadoff walk to Ryan Vilade eventually leading Tracy to pull the plug as Suarez approached 100 pitches. But not before he struck out DeLuca to get the first out.
“He’s a very good competitor and a really good pitcher,” Tracy said, “that even when he’s got traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it. . . . He walked five, but still almost completed six innings. He was very competitive with men on base.”
“I got traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today, and that was part of it,” Suarez said. “It was one of those nights that you didn’t have the command, but I was able to turn the page quickly and was able to get outs when I needed.”
Good as the escape act was, it’s all just staging for what comes next, a playoff berth the Red Sox could clinch on Saturday. Suarez was signed in part because of his experience in the postseason, earned across eight seasons with the Phillies. Suarez is 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 playoff appearances, which includes eight starts. He was the winner of Game 3 of the 2022 World Series, beating the eventual champion Astros with five shutout innings.
The Phillies also called on him to come out of the bullpen in Game 5 of the NLCS, and all he did was earn his first postseason save by getting two outs on two pitches, stranding the winning run and clinching the Series berth.
“When you get to this part of the season, not every outing is going to go perfectly. But he’s been there and done that as far as navigating his way through an outing and finding a way to strand base runners,” Tracy said. “The game’s not going to speed up on him. You know, even if he’s walked some and there’s some people on base, he doesn’t ever look like he speeds up. He just keeps making his pitches.”

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all.
There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings.
But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough.
"I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today and that was part of it."
Suarez had difficulty explaining how the walks piled up on him. It wasn't mechanical, and it wasn't the result of nibbling around the strike zone.
"I think it was one of those nights when I didn't have the command," he said. "But I was able to get outs when I needed."
The latter has always been his calling card. In an era when most starters unleash fastballs at 95 mph or better, Suarez thrives by mixing pitches, keeping hitters off balance and inducing soft contact.
On nights when he can't locate with precision, the margin for error slips further. But again, knowing how to get out of trouble is a mound skill in and of itself.
Suarez has used that talent particularly well in the postseason before, which is part of what motivated the Red Sox to offer him $130 million over five years last winter. Suarez isn't about to come unglued in Yankee Stadium in two weeks — or any other time he gets the ball in the postseason. His career ERA of 1.48 in the playoffs virtually guarantees that.
"He was very competitive with men on base," said interim manager Chad Tracy. "He lost some counts, was behind more counts today, but he wa able to really good pitches with people on base."
Even as he labored, Suarez was adding to a September resumé which has him 3-0 with 0.92 ERA in his last three outings while limiting opposing hitters to a .186 batting average.
No one knows exactly how or when Suarez will fit into Boston's postseason rotation. The assumption is that Sonny Gray will pitch Game 1, with either Payton Tolle or Suarez slotted for Game 2, and the remaining choice available for a winner-take-all Game 3.
Of course, the risk there is that a team may never get to its third starter if it doesn't win at least one of the first two games. That's part of the difficult decision the Red Sox will have to make before their wild card round gets underway.
Even with his history of success in October, Suarez isn't thinking too much about the postseason — not yet anyway.
"No, no,'' he said with a chuckle. "When we clinch, I'll be able to do that. But mathematically, we're not there yet, so I'm not thinking about that."
Suarez has one more start in the regular season, which he can treat as both a tuneup for himself and an audition for Game 2 in the best-of-three wild card round.,
"He's a very good competitor, a good pitcher that even when he gets traffic, you trust that he's going to find his way through it. He does that at times this year, so that's never a concern with him."

Boston Red Sox flamethrower Payton Tolle made his big league debut in 2025 after a meteoric rise through the minors. He quickly made Boston fans fall in love with him because of his blistering fastball, and quirky personality.
Last year, he made it into seven games in the majors. This year, he didn't make the big league out of camp, but he was quickly promoted as injuries popped up elsewhere. Boston's fortunate it made the decision it did to give the lefty a shot because he has been incredible.
So far this season, he has made 25 starts as a rookie and has a 3.02 ERA and a 166-to-38 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 143 innings pitched. If that doesn't impress you enough, he actually is the only rookie in big league history to record a strikeout rate of 28 percent or more and a walk rate of seven percent or lower across at least 140 innings pitched, per Eric Cross of RotoBaller.
Payton Tolle Has Put Together A Historic Rookie Season
"Red Sox Payton Tolle is the only pitcher in MLB history to meet the three thresholds below in their rookie season: 140 innings pitched, strikeout rate above 28 percent, walk rate below 7 percent," Cross wrote.
Terms like "ace" and "No. 1 starter" get tossed around a lot. There aren't many true aces in baseball, or at least not as many as are talked about. While this is the case, Tolle clearly has that type of upside. This is a guy who is just 23 years old. His advanced metrics back up this idea that he can be a legit No. 1 ace.
Right now, he's in the 96th percentile in expected ERA, 93rd percentile in expected batting average against, 96th percentile in chase rate, 98th percentile in extension, 89th percentile in strikeout rate, 94th percentile in fastball run value and the 90th percentile in pitching run value, among many others.
Again, he wasn't even on the Red Sox's Opening Day roster. But he got his opportunity and he has shown clear growth. It has been known that he has an elite fastball. The biggest question for him coming into the 2026 season was whether or not he could develop his secondary pitches. He has done just that, which is a big reason for his overall success.
The Red Sox have a star on their hands, to say the least.

The Boston Red Sox open up a three-game series against AL East rival Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, September 18, at Tropicana Field.
Ranger Suarez will get the ball for Boston tonight. After that, the pitching plans are unclear. The Red Sox have listed TBDs for their starting pitcher spot on Saturday and Sunday, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. Payton Tolle and Patrick Sandoval were lined up to start this weekend, but that is now in doubt.
Probable pitchers for Red Sox-Rays this weekend…
* Friday: Ranger Suarez vs. Ian Seymour* Saturday: TBD vs. Freddy Peralta* Sunday: TBD vs. Griffin Jax
Saturday would be Payton Tolle's day, if the Red Sox stay on turn. We'll see how they handle it.
— Tim Healey (@timbhealey) September 17, 2026
Tolle has already zoomed past his previous career high in innings as a pro. The lefty tossed 108 frames between the minors and majors in 2025. Tolle has thrown 158 innings across both levels this season.
Boston Red Sox May Skip Payton Tolle Against the Tampa Bay Rays
Tolle has been a fixture in Boston's rotation for much of the season. He's posted a 3.03 ERA across 25 starts with the big-league club. The young lefty opened the season in the minors, but was promoted to the majors in April. Tolle has solidified a pitching staff that has dealt with injuries and underperformance at times in 2026.
While he won't win AL Rookie of the Year, Tolle has put together a solid case. He's right up there with Cleveland Guardians left-hander Parker Messick as the top rookie starter in the American League. Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers and Munetaka Murakami of the Chicago White Sox are the betting favorites, but Tolle and Messick will receive some down-ballot votes.
Tolle struggled to a 6.06 ERA in his first taste of the big leagues last year. He missed bats at a decent 25.7% clip, but notched a 10.8% walk rate. The lefty has improved in both departments this season. Tolle pushed his strikeout rate to 28.9% and trimmed his walk rate to 6.6% in his first full campaign as a major league starter.
Red Sox Lining Up Postseason Rotation
Moving Tolle's next start could be an effort to align the playoff rotation. The pitching staff will likely be headlined by Sonny Gray, but the second and third slots are up for grabs. Suarez has a solid case to pitch the second game of the Wild Card round. The gig could also go to Tolle.
Sandoval and Jake Bennett are likely looking at long relief roles in the first round of the playoffs. Both have had decent stretches this season, but faded recently. Bennett has permitted a dozen runs in three September starts. Sandoval has a 7.82 ERA this month.
Brayan Bello is the question mark among the unit. He's struggled as a starter and been tremendous out of the bullpen. Bello could operate in tandem with one of Boston's many left-handed starters.

ARLINGTON, Texas — Nearly three months after Caleb Durbin first dislocated his left pinkie and more than a month after he reinjured it, the third baseman’s digit remains locked nearly at a right angle.
“It doesn’t quite straighten or bend all the way,” Durbin acknowledged.
Durbin received X-rays after his initial injury against the Rockies on June 24 and the reinjury against the White Sox on Aug. 6. In both instances, there was no fracture and he was told playing was simply a matter of pain tolerance.
And so, there was little question about how he’d proceed. He didn’t seek more information.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” he said.
Still, Durbin recognizes fingers shouldn’t look like they could be used to mount a shelf. Might he require offseason surgery?
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
For now, Durbin remains a lineup constant. Thursday’s contest against the Rangers marked his 145th game of the season. He continues to deliver Gold Glove-caliber defense (his six outs above average lead AL third basemen) while also pushing the envelope on the field with high-IQ plays, most recently advancing from first to third on an infield single on Wednesday.
“He plays the game that way,” said Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “It’s what he does.”
Still, it seems the injury is impacting him at the plate. He’s hitting .211/.400/.316 in September — showing fight in his at-bats (thus his standout on-base percentage), but rarely driving the ball. His whiff rate (10 percent of swings) is the lowest for any month this year, but he’s rarely been able to drive the ball. His 48 percent ground ball rate is his highest in any month since May.
But to Durbin, the question of whether or how the injury might be affecting him is secondary. His primary concern is simply whether he is positioned to contribute in any way.
“The pain’s gone down drastically since it happened the second time,” Durbin shrugged. “It’s functional.”
Updates on injured trio
Garrett Crochet, who last threw off a mound on Tuesday, worked out at Polar Park in Worcester on Thursday and will continue to throw on flat ground on Friday before the team decides whether to introduce any higher-intensity activities over the weekend.
Tracy said there’s been no discussion about the lefthander pitching in a rehab game for the WooSox this weekend. He didn’t rule out the possibility Crochet could soon face hitters in a live batting practice session, but made clear that there is no known schedule involving the 27-year-old.
“It all depends on how he’s feeling. … He’s been down so long,” said Tracy. “It is day to day. [Friday he’ll] throw, see how he feels, and then determine what the weekend holds.”
Righthander Tyron Guerrero, whose return from shoulder inflammation was delayed slightly by lower back cramps, had a high-intensity throwing session on flat ground. He’s expected to throw off a mound Friday when the Sox open a three-game series at Tampa Bay, a potential prelude to activation later in the weekend. “The shoulder feels great, the arm feels great,” said Guerrero.
Ceddanne Rafaela is increasing (right quad strain) is increasing his agility work but, at this point, there’s “no discernible timeline yet on game action,” according to Tracy. It hasn’t been determined if Rafaela will join the Sox in Tampa.
Oviedo in Worcester
Righthander Johan Oviedo (right elbow strain), pitching in an official game for the first time since March 30, struck out four batters while sitting at 96 miles per hour and touching 99 with his four-seamer in 2⅓ innings in a rehab appearance for the WooSox. He threw 20 of 30 pitches for strikes … Ranger Suarez will start for the Sox on Friday against the Rays, but the Sox have yet to decide who will start the other two games of the series. Payton Tolle, Patrick Sandoval, and Brayan Bello are all considerations … The Red Sox will send two scouts to New York for next week’s four-game Yankees-Rays series, the start of the team’s in-person advance scouting efforts for the postseason.

Originally viewed as one of the favorites to start the season in the Opening Day rotation, Red Sox right-hander Johan Oviedo wound up making just one appearance out of the bullpen before going on the shelf with a right elbow strain.
Now after missing nearly the entire season, Oviedo may finally be nearing a return.
Oviedo began a rehab assignment at Triple-A Worcester on Thursday, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in his first game action since late March.
The 28-year-old threw 30 pitches, 20 for strikes, while allowing one run on two hits and a walk while striking out four. Oviedo allowed an RBI double with one out in the top of the second before striking out the final three batters he faced.
More encouragingly, Oviedo’s fastball averaged 95.9 mph and topped out at 98.5, a sizable jump from the 92-93 he averaged earlier in the season.
Originally acquired last winter from the Pittsburgh Pirates as part of the Jhostynxon Garcia trade, Oviedo was initially expected to provide rotation depth as a possible high-ceiling power arm. Oviedo had previously missed extensive time due to Tommy John surgery, but finished his last season in Pittsburgh strong with a 3.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts over nine starts down the stretch.
The righty entered spring as one of the favorites for the No. 5 rotation spot, but after some promising early starts began showing signs of wear. The last rotation spot wound up going to Connelly Early, with Oviedo making the team as a reliever, and he made one appearance against the Houston Astros on March 30, allowing four runs over 3 2/3 innings.
Oviedo has been on the injured list ever since, but now he could be a dark horse candidate for the Red Sox playoff roster along with Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet, who are also working their way back from extended injury absences.
Upcoming starters
Ranger Suarez will start Friday’s series opener against the Tampa Bay Rays, but the Red Sox’s other starters remain to be determined. Payton Tolle would normally be in line to start Saturday but Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Texas on Thursday that the club is still deciding how it wants to handle the weekend.
Brayan Bello, who was limited to 19 pitches over 1 2/3 innings on Tuesday, would presumably be a candidate to start one of this weekend’s games.

The Boston Red Sox made one of the very best moves in baseball for the 2026 season, despite the fact that some fans didn't initially believe in the deal.
While searching for a No. 2 starter last offseason, Boston turned to the St. Louis Cardinals and swung a deal for three-time All-Star Sonny Gray. With the Red Sox searching for another elite starter, some wondered if Gray was better suited for a mid-to-back of the rotation spot, rather than the No. 2 spot for a club with World Series aspirations. He has more than delivered and has been Boston's best starter all season. Gray's going to get Cy Young Award votes and Boston should do what it can to try to keep him in town beyond the 2026 season. If he plays, he'll cost a pretty penny. MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo reported that some in the industry believe Gray will get a deal in the range of three years and $75 million — or more — if he continues his career.
"As a free agent, Gray’s renaissance season may position him to receive a lucrative deal that some in the industry expect to match or exceed the three-year, $75 million deal the Rangers gave to Nathan Eovaldi two winters ago," Cotillo wrote. "Interestingly, though, Gray has not committed to pitching again in 2027. In a recent interview with The Boston Globe, Gray said he would retire 'in a heartbeat' if his family signaled that he was wanted back home year-round, even if that meant retiring after the end of this year."
The Red Sox Should Do Everything To Keep Sonny Gray
That's actually also the same deal that the Cardinals gave Gray before the 2024 season as well. He inked a three-year, $75 million pact that he's currently in the final year of. After the season, Gray has a $30 million mutual option for the 2027 season with a $10 million buyout. If Boston picks up its end of the buyout and Gray opts out, then the buyout would be forfeited.
Gray has pitched well enough in a Red Sox uniform to get paid again — if he keeps pitching. So far this season, he has a 17-5 record, 2.76 ERA and 4.0 wins above replacement in 156 2/3 innings pitched. When it comes to Gray, his age stands out at 36 years old. But it hasn't stopped him yet. The price of pitching has gone up in a big way. A deal with a $25 million annual value, as Cotillo pointed out, would be in the range of guys like Michael King, Sean Manaea, and Eovaldi. It would be just above guys like Aaron Nola, Seth Lugo, Robbie Ray and Luis Severino. Gray has been better than all of these guys so far this season.
When it comes to the Red Sox, there isn't as much pitching depth down in the minors as there once was. Over the last year, Boston has traded guys like Hunter Dobbins, Richard Fitts, Brandon Clarke, Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon, among others. Plus, Connelly Early was traded as well.
Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, and Jake Bennett are locks for the 2027 rotation. Johan Oviedo is someone who could play a role. Tanner Houck is another guy who could as well. We've seen all season how impactful injuries are to the rotation. You never have enough arms. A dependable veteran like Gray for the next few years should be a necessity. It's no guarantee that he pitches beyond the 2026 season, but if he does, it should be in a Boston uniform.

The Boston Red Sox could get starting pitcher Tanner Houck prior to the 2026 regular season conclusion, but his postseason availability for the Red Sox remains undecided as the right-hander continues rebuilding his workload following elbow surgery.
MLB.com's official Red Sox injury tracker provided the latest update on his recovery and potential return:
"RHP Tanner Houck Injury: Torn ulnar collateral ligament right elbow/right flexor pronator strain IL date: Feb. 10 (60-day IL) Expected return: Aiming for late regular season Status: Pitched a scoreless inning in his third rehab appearance on Sept. 15 with Triple-A Worcester. Expected to pitch again Sept. 18 trying to reach 45-, 50-pitch range. (Last updated: Sept. 16)"
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Now in his seventh official MLB campaign, Houck has not pitched in a Major League game since May 12, 2025. His previous rehab attempt ended last July before he underwent a hybrid reconstruction of his right ulnar collateral ligament with flexor tendon repair on August 18, 2025.
The Red Sox are preparing the veteran for a relief role rather than asking him to return to the rotation. The best-case scenario would involve Houck appearing in one or two games during the final week of the regular season before a potential postseason roster decision.
There is still no guarantee that happens. Houck's third rehab appearance came Tuesday with Triple-A Worcester, when he struck out three and walked one during a scoreless inning. He threw 22 pitches, 11 for strikes, and reached 94.2 mph with his fastball.
He also worked out of the bullpen during Boston's 2021 postseason run, making five relief appearances and throwing 10.1 innings, experience that could ease a short-term transition in October.
Houck is expected to pitch Friday and work into the 45- to 50-pitch range. His performance and recovery from that outing will help determine whether a late-season return remains realistic and whether the Red Sox consider him worthy of receiving a spot on the postseason bullpen role.

Good morning! Last night, Jake Bennett was unable to hold the Rangers in check during the team's 7-3 loss in Texas. Some of his numbers look good (seven strikeouts against just one walk), but he also surrendered eight hits in just 4.2 innings, which did in his evening.
With just ten games left in the season, the question now becomes how should the Sox use Bennett going forward? With some combination of Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez likely to get lined up in a best of three Wild Card Series, do you just hold Bennett on the sidelines and hope he gets to come back into the fold as a fourth starter in the ALDS or even ALCS? Or do you start transitioning him to some sort of relief role?
It's a bit of an awkward moment for Bennett. He's been getting knocked around during his last two outings while Suarez is seemingly getting locked in. It almost certainly cuts him out of the Wild Card rotation, and if the Sox get some combination of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Tyron Guerrero back to add to Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller in the bullpen, Bennett largely gets squeezed out of relevance.
So how do you want him used? Do those six shutout innings Bennett threw against the Yankees back on August 29th make you want the Sox to find a role for him if they play New York? Do you think he's just a young pitcher who looks out of gas and want to hide him until the team needs a fourth starter?
Use this space to talk about Bennett and the rest of the difficult upcoming pitching staff decisions, and, as always, be good to one another.
